text_fidelity_a:
Sony HT-A5000 5.1.2ch Dolby Atmos Sound Bar Surround Sound Home Theater with DTS:X and 360 Spatial Sound Mapping, works with Alexa and Google Assistant,Black This arrived well packaged and without issues. I've tried out several major brand soundbars in recent years, and I've yet to find any that are as good as the Sonys, at least as a television speaker. I've already got an A7000 that I'm familiar with to compare this A5000 with. It's a step down in price and feature set, but there's more to the differences than that.

The A7000 has cloth speaker covers on top, while this A5000 has plastic. It's my impression that the sound is a bit better out of the cloth, since it provides less of a reflective barrier, but it's also hard to keep clean and safe. Being on top of the speaker facing up, it's right where something can get pur or dropped on it, or a cat walking across it. The hard plastic seems much more resilient. It's also hard to tell on the sound, because the A5000 has two fewer speakers.

The top of this speaker is a textured plastic, like a car's dashboard. Not super fancy, but resilient. The A7000 has very shiny black plastic, which looks very nice and is easy to clean, but also lacks resilience and shows dust more readily.

The remote is infrared, so you need to have line of sight to the speaker for it to work, but it's full featured, even having buttons to control optional additional speakers. which I really appreciate.

The instruction book is pretty good. Setup is easy, especially if you connect it to a television. It'll put the menus right up on the screen. It's really built to be a television speaker with bluetooth and other inputs so it can be used for other things as a secondary purpose.

I'm still trying to figure out what I can do with the Chromecast feature that seems to be present in the speaker, but not in the television. So far I haven't had much luck connecting with Chromecast.

I definitely like the A7000 better, but there's a solid price difference. I love having a second HDMI input, since the way they've got these things set up, it outputs to my Sony television rather than the other way around, so I need to plug in extra devices to the soundbar, not the television, which makes it a weird decision to put so many more ports on the television than the speaker.

Great speaker, but still plenty of things that could be improved in a future version, like more satellite speaker compatibility, some kind of port passthrough from television, chromecast video, etc.
text_fidelity_b: Sony HT-A5000 5.1.2ch Dolby Atmos Sound Bar Surround Sound Home Theater with DTS:X and 360 Spatial Sound Mapping, works with Alexa and Google Assistant,Black

Except for the visual display of time and date, I could have accomplished everything I mentioned with my old hockey puck, A.K.A. "Dot." At any rate I use this a LOT more than I did the Dot.

The real user in the house if my wife. She is constantly interacting with her Echo, but she was the household power user when she was using a Dot as well. While I feel as though I have gotten my money's worth from mine, the truth is my wife's daily (hourly?) use of hers makes the pair we have in our own home work spaces a bargain.

Bottom line: cool device that has numerous uses - many of which I don't personally use. For some reason the screen inspires me to use mine a lot more than the screenless Dot, and honestly I rarely use the Echo visually.

text_fidelity_a: HPRT MT800 Wireless Bluetooth Monochrome Portable Printer, Case+Cartridge+Printer，Supports 8.5" X 11" US Letter,Compatible with Android and iOS Phone, No-Ink Technology.(MT800QC) I have always wanted a little printer like this when I was working many years ago but they were never this small.  Now that I go camping in my RV and work while I camp I may want to print something without having to drag a full size printer along for the ride.  The price of this is on the high side even higher than the average full size printer so you better have a need to make it worth it.  Don't do what I did which was to unwrap everything before I ready the manual.  I thought I would have to install the enclosed ribbon but it is already installed at the factory and the one you see is a spare.  I decided to set it up to print from my phone since I mainly use a phone or tablet when on the road.  I downloaded the suggested app and it was easy to get started and I didn't need to sign up or register to do so.  My Bluetooth found it right away.  I selected first to print a photo file and selected low quality as I didn't want to waste ink.  It came out OK.  I next selected a page in a PDF manual that had a [photo embedded in it and selected medium quality and that turned out great.  The only gripe was it only gave me the following places to look for a file to print:  iCloud, Photo, Web and my print history.  I only had a couple things in iCloud as I mainly use Google Drive so I would have to move the document to iCloud first in order to print it.  Photo didn't allow me to browse my photos so I wasn't dure where to go there.  Once I printed a photo inn iCloud then that photo showed up there to print in the future.  I thought that was what the print history was for.  So, the app could use some UI work but I can't complain as everything worked/connected so easily.  Now, the paper.  You have to use their HPRT Premium Multi-Purpose Copy Paper.  It is a bit shiny on one side and more expensive than typical print paper.  This brings me back to you have to really need a niche printer like this to make it worth it.  I cannot sweat these things because I got it to use sparingly while I travel when something just has to be in print form.  I don't even really print much anymore from my home printer so once could say I waste cartridges there.  In summary, if you need a portable printer, that costs more with proprietary paper, for those short run printing emergencies on the road then this is great.  It works great and is easy to setup.
text_fidelity_b: HPRT MT800 Wireless Bluetooth Monochrome Portable Printer, Case+Cartridge+Printer，Supports 8.5" X 11" US Letter,Compatible with Android and iOS Phone, No-Ink Technology.(MT800QC)

Garmin nüvi 360 3.5-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator with Text-To-Speech (Discontinued by Manufacturer) I've had this Nuvi 360 since Dec, 2006. It really works well. I carried it with me to DC. Even on foot it was terrific. It knew where all the restaurants and points of interest were and faithfully navigated us around the ancient horse paths of the Virginia/DC area. Believe me, when you pop out of an underground Metro station in the middle of the night and have no idea where you are or which direction to head off in, the ol' Garmin was there.

It's so small it easily fits in a pocket. The built-in battery lasts reasonably long. In the car, the 12-Volt adapter allows the unit to stay on indefinitely. You can select which accent and which gender you want the voice prompts to speak. Australian "Bruce," American "Jill" and a host of other combinations. All very fun. The voice prompts are the best. You really don't need to look at the thing while driving because it's uncanny in telling you what to do when you need to do it. It is amazingly accurate: something like 20 feet. It takes you right to the destination driveway.

It acquires the sats quickly and doesn't get flustered if you violate its recommendation and go in a different route. It just says, "recalculating" and finds another route for you. None of this "make a U-turn, bonehead!" It gives you enough time to make the turns, too. Also, it displays how far it is until the next turn. Very nice. No need to worry if you've missed it.

If you are planning on going to Europe, buy the unit that comes preloaded with both US and Europe maps as purchasing the Europe maps after the fact will really jump the cost unnecessarily.

I haven't used the Bluetooth capability yet but might later...after I get a Bluetooth phone.

The display is quite viewable in daylight and very bright at night, though it can be set to auto-dim at sundown so it's not too bright at night. You can touch the screen and scroll the map under your finger much like Google Maps can, to preview your route if desired. It shows coordinates and you can save them as destinations if desired, even if the location doesn't have an official street address. It is an MP3 player and can display photos and play Audible books on tape. When you are using the MP3 or Audible features, it pauses the file playing back to announce directions, then returns to the file without losing any of the MP3 file or book info. Very nice.

At extra cost, it has the ability to add foreign language dictionaries which can verbally speak phrases and words to you. You can also add Travel Guides and other software via the SD chip slot.

Overall, I'm very pleased with this device. It's accurate, fast, functional and small.

The one thing that doesn't work is the windshield suction mount. It broke before I even used it once. The plastic loops on the suction cup that receive the ball arm's hinge pin are too thin and fragile and broke with just a little normal hinge adjustment.

I recommend the model 010-10908-00 friction mount that looks like a bean bag with a ball arm sticking up. I made something similar by taking an unneeded 1/4" thick mousepad and epoxying a couple of small 1" x 1" angle brackets to the pad to hold the ball arm that I salvaged from the broken suction cup mount.

A friction mount is interchangeable with multiple vehicles, doesn't slide around on the dash and allows complete and rapid removal and/or hiding to avoid theft. Plus, you don't have to glue a disk to the dash for the suction cup to attach to.

UPDATE 10-22-07:
The 360 works well enough; better than most. It should: Five point three bills should deliver one heck of a map!

I've had it since Dec 2006...less than one year. Today I get an offer from Garmin to update my North American map software for a mere point seven bills. That's AFTER the five point three bills I already sunk into this little electronic gizmo.

I heard Garmin has a one year free map update policy, but their website won't let me do it. Not cool. The cost of the unit has already fallen significantly from what I originally paid and now they want more to get it current, within a year of purchase. Not cool at all. Also, impossible to contact by email. Garmin website is in a permanent loop back to itself when clicking on the "contact by email" option. Otherwise, it's call and wait on hold between certain times. Not cool again.

Then a friend says how well his Verizon GPS works on his wireless phone. I look into that. Verizon offers a full time GPS cost and a single use option for under three bucks per use.

For what I have wasted on this Garmin--over five bills and counting upward forever with their unfriendly updates--that's a whole heck of a lot of one-time Verizon uses with what will be the most updated, most accurate database. After all, no one's going to beat the phone company with accurate phone numbers and addresses.

If I hadn't already bought into the Garmin ripoff, I'd definitely go with Verizon's phone based GPS: the phone will always be with you when you need it instead of in the glove compartment in the other car.

And it most likely won't get stolen. It's a darned pain to have to put the Garmin away after each use so some cretin won't bash in a window to steal a very, very expensive toy that could just as easily fit inside a phone.

Go with the phone.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin nüvi 360 3.5-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator with Text-To-Speech (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

text_fidelity_a:
Lenovo IdeaCentre 3 Desktop Tower, AMD Athlon Silver 3050U, AMD Radeon Graphics, 4GB DDR4, 256GB SSD, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, HDMI, Windows 10 You may know about the announcement from Lenovo a few weeks ago that going forward the company will be certifying all their ThinkPad and Thinkstation workstations for Linux. This computer is an IdeaCentre, not a ThinkPad or ThinkStation, and it comes preloaded with Windows, but I am a Linux user and I wanted to see if it will run Linux.

First things first: If you're looking for a gaming computer or something to handle graphics-intensive programs, this isn't it. It doesn't have a screaming fast processor, although it is a capable one. The onboard AMD Raven graphics module is pretty capable (I tried it out on a big display), but this model has no expansion slot for a video or audio card or any other such upgrades.

It does have a bay for a big 3.5 inch HDD with SATA connectors. And it comes with a 256GB SSD already installed on the motherboard. It also comes with 4GB RAM (and a second slot to add more), and a wired keyboard and mouse and the power supply. It has four USB 2.0 ports in the back, and two 2.0 and two 3.0 (gen 1) USB ports in the front. Also on the front are a card reader slot, the optical drive, mic and headset connection ports, and the power button. The back also has an HDMI port, VGA-out port, and and ethernet port.

It's about the size of an ITX mini tower form factor box, which is a little larger than a big dictionary. It stands upright, so the footprint is pretty small. And it's lightweight compared to a big desktop box.

I didn't even complete the first boot into Windows before attempting a Linux install. Tapping F2 on boot will get you into a graphical menu for picking your boot device, and F12 will get you into a deeper menu for selecting boot order and into the BIOS.

My favorite distro is Debian, so I thought I'd take a shot at installing it. It was a no-go. It didn't have the drivers for the onboard Atheros wifi card, and apparently a few other things. I actually pulled the wifi card off the motherboard and substituted a dongle and gave it a second try. I got Debian installed, but the machine still froze on boot without ever getting into the desktop environment.

So I tried installing Ubuntu, which, along with Red Hat, was specifically mentioned as now being supported by Lenovo. Success. Installation went smoothly. I was still using the dongle for wifi, so I shut down the machine and reinstalled the inboard card. Again, success. Wifi operated right away.

The couple of minor -- emphasizing minor -- things I don't like is that an inboard white LED glows continually when the power supply is plugged in, and as far as I can tell there's no way to turn it off.

Bottom line here is I think it's a good machine for general use. It's pretty capable, but be aware of its limitations so you won't be disappointed.
text_fidelity_b: Lenovo IdeaCentre 3 Desktop Tower, AMD Athlon Silver 3050U, AMD Radeon Graphics, 4GB DDR4, 256GB SSD, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, HDMI, Windows 10

I was amazed by the price when I came onto Amazon to check - $29.99 was a steal compared to the $80 we spent a few years back! This headset is not the top of the line, but it is effective in canceling out the low aircraft drawl while in-flight. (They are also quite nice when you need to drown out the crying child in 23F. ;)) The battery life is remarkable. I have had to change the battery on my set only twice in the three years I've owned it. The only complaint that I have, which results in the four star rating instead of five, is that after wearing the set for a few hours (i.e., Amsterdam to Houston, TX), my ears begin to ache on the outside. It is almost like the headset becomes to tight over longer periods of time. I tend not to wear earrings on airplanes, so I can rule out the possibility of pinching. Other than that slight achy feeling, these are wonderful for the casual traveler and the price simply cannot be beat!

text_fidelity_a:
Antennas Direct DB2 Multi Directional HDTV Antenna (Discontinued by Manufacturer) I recently purchase an Antenna's Direct Clearstream 4 to use in my attic to feed the TVs in the BR and LR. Works fantastic, so when I needed another antenna for a TV in the study that I could not hook up to the antenna in the attic, I again went with Antenna's Direct, but this time picked the DB2 since it was smaller (and cheaper).

Absolutely fantastic reception! The only station it does not pull in as well as the Clearstream 4 was one fringe station. As with the Clearstream 4 positioning is a breeze - I just propped it up in the corner!

Given how well it performs, I thought I'd see how it does in the attic in place of the much larger and more expensive Clearstream. It does nearly as well - all the major networks come in equally good, and the DB2 picks up all but one of the more distant stations. The one it misses is a channel I never watch anyway, so for me, the two are equal.

For me (located outside Wash DC) the antennas pull in 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 5, 7.1, 7.2, 7.3, 9.1, 9.2, 14.1, 20.1, and about a dozen PBS stations rock solid. Channels 66.1 to 66.4 are so-so on the DB2 and pretty good on the Clearstream 4.

The Clearstream 4 also pulls in several analog stations. I didn't try that with the DB2 so I don't know if it will work with analog. Come February, the point will be moot anyway, so I didn't bother to test it out for analog.

So, if you're debating between the Clearstream 4 and the DB2 (or DB4), give the DB2 a shot first - the little guy may do the trick, and you can save quite a bit of cash.
text_fidelity_b: Antennas Direct DB2 Multi Directional HDTV Antenna (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

text_fidelity_a: GEEKOM Mini AIR11 Mini PC Windows 11, 8GB RAM Dual DDR4 256GB M.2 SSD, Mini NUC Computer with Intel 11th Gen N5095, Home/Business Mini Desktop Computer, 4K UHD/Dual WiFi/BT4.2/HDMI/Gigabit Ethernet It amazes me just how much power this little computer has.  It runs silently and generates almost no heat.  So far I have only used it with Wi-Fi and the performance has been quite good.  I want to try it with an ethernet cable, directly connected to see if performance is even better.  The biggest struggle that I had in dealing with this computer is that it has Windows 11 installed.  Not being familiar with 11, since all my other PCs have Win 10, I had a hard time finding some commonly used functions.  Of course that is not the fault of the computer.  There are some things to be aware of if you buy this.  First of all, you need a monitor, keyboard and mouse to use with the computer, since it doesn't come with these items.  Secondly, the computer seems to use all the latest connection types, such as HDMI for video.  All but one of my monitors don't have HDMI, but only DVI and/or VGA connectors.  If you don't have an HDMI connection on your monitor, you will need an adapter or adapter cable that converts the type of connector that you have to HDMI.  There is an included HDMI cable, with both ends HDMI.  There also is a mini display port connector, which I am not familiar with.  The mouse and keyboard could be another issue.  All my mice use the round PS/2 type connectors and some of my available keyboards are the same way with the old PS/2 connector.  To connect to the Geekom, you either need a USB keyboard and mouse (which will use up 2 of the 3 available USB ports) or your need a wireless keyboard and mouse.  Wireless may use one or two USB ports, depending on whether the receiver for the mouse and keyboard is integrated to handle both or if you have a keyboard and a mouse from different manufacturers, which requires two receivers, instead of one.  A good feature this computer has is a mounting bracket that allows you to mount it to the back of certain monitors, which is a space saver.  You really don't need this, as the computer is so small anyway that the footprint is minimal.  The only thing I would have liked on this is a DVI connector.  Also, the manual is very minimal.  Currently the computer goes to sleep after a few minutes and I have to press the power button to get it to wake up.  This could be normal behavior and I have an inquiry in to Geekom to find out.  I love this little computer and I will probably never buy a full sized computer again.  Storage is limited, but I keep all my data on external network drives and backed up to the cloud, so a lot of storage on the computer is not an issue these days.  If you can deal with the newer connection types with this computer, I think you will really love it.  I am really happy with it.  It is hard to find anything wrong with this computer.  I think it seems to be quite sturdy too, as the UPS delivery man just dropped the package with a big thump by my front door.  I was afraid it might damage the computer, but it worked fine, so I guess it can handle some bumps and thumps, as it was not packed with a lot of cushioning material.
text_fidelity_b: GEEKOM Mini AIR11 Mini PC Windows 11, 8GB RAM Dual DDR4 256GB M.2 SSD, Mini NUC Computer with Intel 11th Gen N5095, Home/Business Mini Desktop Computer, 4K UHD/Dual WiFi/BT4.2/HDMI/Gigabit Ethernet
